Topic 06·Anik Sir · Lecture 7

Fourier transform

Spectra of aperiodic signals, the standard pairs, properties, duality and bandwidth.

18 past questions on this topic

Beyond periodic signals

The Fourier series decomposes periodic signals: it needs x(t+T)=x(t)x(t+T)=x(t)x(t+T)=x(t). But many real signals never repeat. A clap, a single data pulse, a heartbeat recorded once: one-time events with no fixed period.

Can we still describe a non-repeating signal using frequencies? Yes. The Fourier transform does for aperiodic signals what the Fourier series does for periodic ones.

From series to transform: let the period go to infinity

Cheat first: repeat one lonely pulse

Start with one finite-duration signal x(t)x(t)x(t) and repeat it every TTT:

xT(t)=∑m=−∞∞x(t−mT).x_T(t)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}x(t-mT).xT​(t)=m=−∞∑∞​x(t−mT).

Now it is periodic, so the Fourier series works. As TTT grows the copies move away from each other, and as T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞ the repeated signal looks like one isolated pulse.

What happens in frequency?

The allowed frequencies are kω0k\omega_0kω0​ with ω0=2πT\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}Tω0​=T2π​. Small TTT means large spacing and few lines; large TTT means tiny spacing and many lines. Increasing TTT packs the allowed frequencies closer and closer together.

A smooth spectrum is hiding behind the stems

The series coefficients of xTx_TxT​ are

ak=1T∫−T/2T/2xT(t)e−jkω0tdt=1T∫−∞∞x(t)e−jkω0tdt,\begin{aligned}&a_k\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}x_T(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t}dt\\[6pt]&= \frac1T\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t}dt,\end{aligned}​ak​=T1​∫−T/2T/2​xT​(t)e−jkω0​tdt=T1​∫−∞∞​x(t)e−jkω0​tdt,​

because inside one period xTx_TxT​ is just the isolated pulse x(t)x(t)x(t), and the pulse is zero outside. The integral depends on kkk only through kω0k\omega_0kω0​. Give it a name:

X(jω)=∫−∞∞x(t)e−jωtdt⟹T ak=X(jkω0).X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad T\,a_k=X(jk\omega_0).X(jω)=∫−∞∞​x(t)e−jωtdt⟹Tak​=X(jkω0​).

The stems are samples of one smooth curve. As TTT increases, the sample points kω0k\omega_0kω0​ crowd together until they trace out the whole curve.

Why do the raw coefficients shrink?

ak=1TX(jkω0)a_k=\frac1TX(jk\omega_0)ak​=T1​X(jkω0​), and since Δω=ω0=2πT\Delta\omega=\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}TΔω=ω0​=T2π​, we have 1T=Δω2π\frac1T=\frac{\Delta\omega}{2\pi}T1​=2πΔω​. Think of it as a frequency density: each stem's amount is spread over a bin of width Δω\Delta\omegaΔω. As Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 the bins get thinner and the discrete spectrum becomes continuous.

The sum becomes an integral

Start from the series and substitute ak=Δω2πX(jkω0)a_k=\frac{\Delta\omega}{2\pi}X(jk\omega_0)ak​=2πΔω​X(jkω0​):

xT(t)=∑kakejkω0t=12π∑kX(jkω0) ejkω0t Δω.\begin{aligned}&x_T(t)\\[6pt]&= \sum_ka_ke^{jk\omega_0t}\\[6pt]&= \frac1{2\pi}\sum_kX(jk\omega_0)\,e^{jk\omega_0t}\,\Delta\omega .\end{aligned}​xT​(t)=k∑​ak​ejkω0​t=2π1​k∑​X(jkω0​)ejkω0​tΔω.​

Let T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞: Δω→dω\Delta\omega\to d\omegaΔω→dω, kω0→ωk\omega_0\to\omegakω0​→ω becomes a continuous variable, xT→xx_T\to xxT​→x, and the sum becomes an integral.

The Fourier transform pair

 X(jω)=∫−∞∞x(t) e−jωt dt (analysis)\boxed{\,X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,e^{-j\omega t}\,dt\,}\qquad\text{(analysis)}X(jω)=∫−∞∞​x(t)e−jωtdt​(analysis)  x(t)=12π∫−∞∞X(jω) ejωt dω (synthesis)\boxed{\,x(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}X(j\omega)\,e^{j\omega t}\,d\omega\,}\qquad\text{(synthesis)}x(t)=2π1​∫−∞∞​X(jω)ejωtdω​(synthesis)

We write x(t)↔X(jω)x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)x(t)↔X(jω).

The Fourier transform is not a new idea. It is the Fourier series after the frequency lines become continuous. Periodic signals have discrete spectra; aperiodic signals have continuous spectra; and the series coefficients of a periodic extension are samples of the single pulse's transform.

In hertz. With ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf the pair becomes G(f)=∫g(t)e−j2πftdtG(f)=\int g(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}dtG(f)=∫g(t)e−j2πftdt, g(t)=∫G(f)ej2πftdfg(t)=\int G(f)e^{j2\pi ft}dfg(t)=∫G(f)ej2πftdf with no 12π\frac1{2\pi}2π1​. The CSE 311 papers use this form; everything below carries over with ω→2πf\omega\to2\pi fω→2πf.

Injecting oscillation: the frequency-shift property

What happens to the spectrum if we put an oscillation inside a signal, x(t)→x(t)cos⁡ω0tx(t)\to x(t)\cos\omega_0tx(t)→x(t)cosω0​t? The shape of x(t)x(t)x(t) becomes an envelope, with the cosine oscillating inside. A damped pendulum, a vibrating string with loss, a ringing circuit and a fading echo all look like this.

Solve the cleaner version first: x(t)ejω0tx(t)e^{j\omega_0t}x(t)ejω0​t. A frequency component of xxx looks like ejωte^{j\omega t}ejωt; after multiplying,

ejωt⋅ejω0t=ej(ω+ω0)t,e^{j\omega t}\cdot e^{j\omega_0t}=e^{j(\omega+\omega_0)t},ejωt⋅ejω0​t=ej(ω+ω0​)t,

so every component at ω\omegaω moves to ω+ω0\omega+\omega_0ω+ω0​. The spectrum slides to the right:

 x(t)ejω0t ↔ X(j(ω−ω0)) \boxed{\,x(t)e^{j\omega_0t}\ \leftrightarrow\ X\big(j(\omega-\omega_0)\big)\,}x(t)ejω0​t ↔ X(j(ω−ω0​))​

(To move a spectrum right by ω0\omega_0ω0​ we write X(j(ω−ω0))X(j(\omega-\omega_0))X(j(ω−ω0​)): the same "minus means right" rule as time shifting.)

Cosine modulation

A cosine is two rotating exponentials, cos⁡ω0t=12(ejω0t+e−jω0t)\cos\omega_0t=\frac12(e^{j\omega_0t}+e^{-j\omega_0t})cosω0​t=21​(ejω0​t+e−jω0​t), so

x(t)cos⁡ω0t=12x(t)ejω0t+12x(t)e−jω0t ↔ 12X(j(ω−ω0))+12X(j(ω+ω0)).x(t)\cos\omega_0t=\tfrac12x(t)e^{j\omega_0t}+\tfrac12x(t)e^{-j\omega_0t}\ \leftrightarrow\ \tfrac12X\big(j(\omega-\omega_0)\big)+\tfrac12X\big(j(\omega+\omega_0)\big).x(t)cosω0​t=21​x(t)ejω0​t+21​x(t)e−jω0​t ↔ 21​X(j(ω−ω0​))+21​X(j(ω+ω0​)).

In time we injected an oscillation. In frequency the spectrum moved to ±ω0\pm\omega_0±ω0​ as two half-height copies. This is how AM radio and every frequency-division system work.

The rectangle: a transform to keep in your toolbox

x(t)={1,−T2<t<T20,otherwisex(t)=\begin{cases}1,&-\frac T2<t<\frac T2\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(t)={1,0,​−2T​<t<2T​otherwise​

X(jω)=∫−T/2T/2e−jωtdt=[e−jωt−jω]−T/2T/2=ejωT/2−e−jωT/2jω=2sin⁡(ωT/2)ω\begin{aligned}&X(j\omega)\\[6pt]&= \int_{-T/2}^{T/2}e^{-j\omega t}dt\\[6pt]&= \left[\frac{e^{-j\omega t}}{-j\omega}\right]_{-T/2}^{T/2}\\[6pt]&= \frac{e^{j\omega T/2}-e^{-j\omega T/2}}{j\omega}\\[6pt]&= \boxed{\frac{2\sin(\omega T/2)}{\omega}}\end{aligned}​X(jω)=∫−T/2T/2​e−jωtdt=[−jωe−jωt​]−T/2T/2​=jωejωT/2−e−jωT/2​=ω2sin(ωT/2)​​​

  • The peak at ω=0\omega=0ω=0 is TTT, the area of the rectangle.
  • Zeros at ω=2πkT\omega=\frac{2\pi k}Tω=T2πk​, k=±1,±2,…k=\pm1,\pm2,\dotsk=±1,±2,…; the main lobe is 4πT\frac{4\pi}{T}T4π​ wide.
  • The side lobes decay like 1/∣ω∣1/|\omega|1/∣ω∣: the sharp edges need high frequencies.

Wider rectangle, narrower spectrum. Large TTT squeezes the main lobe.

A Lego-block signal

x(t)={1,1<t<21.5,2<t<31,3<t<40,otherwisex(t)=\begin{cases}1,&1<t<2\\1.5,&2<t<3\\1,&3<t<4\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}x(t)=⎩⎨⎧​1,1.5,1,0,​1<t<22<t<33<t<4otherwise​

Decompose: a height-1 block of width 3 centred at 2.5, plus a height-0.5 block of width 1 centred at 2.5.

X(jω)=e−j2.5ω 2sin⁡1.5ωω+0.5 e−j2.5ω 2sin⁡0.5ωω=e−j2.5ω 2sin⁡1.5ω+sin⁡0.5ωω.\begin{aligned}&X(j\omega)\\[6pt]&= e^{-j2.5\omega}\,\frac{2\sin1.5\omega}{\omega}+0.5\,e^{-j2.5\omega}\,\frac{2\sin0.5\omega}{\omega}\\[6pt]&= e^{-j2.5\omega}\,\frac{2\sin1.5\omega+\sin0.5\omega}{\omega}.\end{aligned}​X(jω)=e−j2.5ωω2sin1.5ω​+0.5e−j2.5ωω2sin0.5ω​=e−j2.5ωω2sin1.5ω+sin0.5ω​.​

Lock a cosine inside the rectangle

x(t)=r(t)cos⁡ω0tx(t)=r(t)\cos\omega_0tx(t)=r(t)cosω0​t, a windowed cosine, is just modulation of a rectangle:

X(jω)=sin⁡((ω−ω0)T/2)ω−ω0+sin⁡((ω+ω0)T/2)ω+ω0.X(j\omega)=\frac{\sin\big((\omega-\omega_0)T/2\big)}{\omega-\omega_0}+\frac{\sin\big((\omega+\omega_0)T/2\big)}{\omega+\omega_0}.X(jω)=ω−ω0​sin((ω−ω0​)T/2)​+ω+ω0​sin((ω+ω0​)T/2)​.

A cosine inside a rectangle has a spectrum centred at ±ω0\pm\omega_0±ω0​, not at zero. The longer the window, the narrower each copy: a pure tone of infinite length would give two impulses.

The transform of a spike

x(t)=δ(t)x(t)=\delta(t)x(t)=δ(t). By the sifting property, the impulse samples e−jωte^{-j\omega t}e−jωt at t=0t=0t=0:

X(jω)=∫−∞∞δ(t)e−jωtdt=e−jω⋅0=1.\begin{aligned}&X(j\omega)\\[6pt]&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\\[6pt]&= e^{-j\omega\cdot0}\\[6pt]&= 1 .\end{aligned}​X(jω)=∫−∞∞​δ(t)e−jωtdt=e−jω⋅0=1.​

A very narrow spike in time needs all frequencies equally. Bonus: a shifted spike δ(t−t0)\delta(t-t_0)δ(t−t0​) samples the exponential at t0t_0t0​, so δ(t−t0)↔e−jωt0\delta(t-t_0)\leftrightarrow e^{-j\omega t_0}δ(t−t0​)↔e−jωt0​: flat magnitude, linear phase.

Time shift: delay means linear phase

∫x(t−t0)e−jωtdt =τ=t−t0 e−jωt0∫x(τ)e−jωτdτ=e−jωt0X(jω).\int x(t-t_0)e^{-j\omega t}dt\ \overset{\tau=t-t_0}{=}\ e^{-j\omega t_0}\int x(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau}d\tau=e^{-j\omega t_0}X(j\omega).∫x(t−t0​)e−jωtdt =τ=t−t0​ e−jωt0​∫x(τ)e−jωτdτ=e−jωt0​X(jω).

The magnitude is untouched; the phase gains −ωt0-\omega t_0−ωt0​, a straight line through the origin. Each frequency component is delayed by the same t0t_0t0​ because higher frequencies get proportionally more phase.

Scaling: compress in time, expand in frequency

x(at)↔1∣a∣X ⁣(jωa).x(at)\leftrightarrow\frac1{|a|}X\!\left(\frac{j\omega}{a}\right).x(at)↔∣a∣1​X(ajω​).

For a>0a>0a>0 substitute τ=at\tau=atτ=at: ∫x(at)e−jωtdt=1a∫x(τ)e−j(ω/a)τdτ\int x(at)e^{-j\omega t}dt=\frac1a\int x(\tau)e^{-j(\omega/a)\tau}d\tau∫x(at)e−jωtdt=a1​∫x(τ)e−j(ω/a)τdτ. For a<0a<0a<0 the limits swap, giving ∣a∣|a|∣a∣.

Time–bandwidth reciprocity. A signal that is narrow in time is wide in frequency, and vice versa. Playing a tape at double speed halves its duration and doubles every pitch. A signal cannot be both time-limited and band-limited.

Differentiation

Differentiate the synthesis integral; only ejωte^{j\omega t}ejωt depends on ttt:

dxdt=12π∫(jω)X(jω)ejωtdω⟹dxdt↔jωX(jω).\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac1{2\pi}\int(j\omega)X(j\omega)e^{j\omega t}d\omega\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\frac{dx}{dt}\leftrightarrow j\omega X(j\omega).dtdx​=2π1​∫(jω)X(jω)ejωtdω⟹dtdx​↔jωX(jω).

So a differentiator is an LTI system with H(jω)=jωH(j\omega)=j\omegaH(jω)=jω. It boosts high frequencies in proportion to ∣ω∣|\omega|∣ω∣, so a derivative has its energy shifted to higher frequencies.

Convolution theorem

F{x∗h}=∫ ⁣ ⁣∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ e−jωtdt=∫x(τ)e−jωτ[∫h(t−τ)e−jω(t−τ)dt]dτ=X(jω)H(jω).\begin{aligned}&\mathcal F\{x*h\}\\[6pt]&= \int\!\!\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau\,e^{-j\omega t}dt\\[6pt]&= \int x(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau}\left[\int h(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega(t-\tau)}dt\right]d\tau\\[6pt]&= X(j\omega)H(j\omega).\end{aligned}​F{x∗h}=∫∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτe−jωtdt=∫x(τ)e−jωτ[∫h(t−τ)e−jω(t−τ)dt]dτ=X(jω)H(jω).​

Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency. By duality, multiplication in time is convolution in frequency (with 12π\frac1{2\pi}2π1​).

Duality

The analysis and synthesis integrals have the same shape. From the synthesis equation, 2πx(−t)=∫X(jω)e−jωtdω2\pi x(-t)=\int X(j\omega)e^{-j\omega t}d\omega2πx(−t)=∫X(jω)e−jωtdω; swapping the names ttt and ω\omegaω:

x(t)↔X(jω)⟹X(jt)↔2π x(−ω).x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X(jt)\leftrightarrow2\pi\,x(-\omega).x(t)↔X(jω)⟹X(jt)↔2πx(−ω).

Every pair comes with a free twin: rectangle ↔ sinc gives sinc ↔ rectangle, δ(t)↔1\delta(t)\leftrightarrow1δ(t)↔1 gives 1↔2πδ(ω)1\leftrightarrow2\pi\delta(\omega)1↔2πδ(ω), triangle ↔ sinc² gives sinc² ↔ triangle.

Symmetry of real signals

If xxx is real,

X∗(jω)=∫x(t)e+jωtdt=X(−jω)\begin{aligned}&X^*(j\omega)\\[6pt]&= \int x(t)e^{+j\omega t}dt\\[6pt]&= X(-j\omega)\end{aligned}​X∗(jω)=∫x(t)e+jωtdt=X(−jω)​

In polar form:

∣X(−jω)∣=∣X(jω)∣  (magnitude even),∠X(−jω)=−∠X(jω)  (phase odd).|X(-j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)|\ \ (\text{magnitude even}),\qquad\angle X(-j\omega)=-\angle X(j\omega)\ \ (\text{phase odd}).∣X(−jω)∣=∣X(jω)∣  (magnitude even),∠X(−jω)=−∠X(jω)  (phase odd).

Real and even signals have real, even spectra; real and odd signals have imaginary, odd spectra.

The sign function: a transform defined as a limit

sgn⁡(t)=−1\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1sgn(t)=−1 for t<0t<0t<0 and +1+1+1 for t>0t>0t>0. It is not absolutely integrable, so integrate a family that tends to it. With f(t)=e−atu(t)f(t)=e^{-at}u(t)f(t)=e−atu(t) (a>0a>0a>0):

f(t)↔1a+jω,f(−t)=eatu(−t)↔1a−jω(time reversal),f(t)\leftrightarrow\frac1{a+j\omega},\qquad f(-t)=e^{at}u(-t)\leftrightarrow\frac1{a-j\omega}\quad(\text{time reversal}),f(t)↔a+jω1​,f(−t)=eatu(−t)↔a−jω1​(time reversal),

Then u(t)=12+12sgn⁡(t)↔πδ(ω)+1jωu(t)=\frac12+\frac12\operatorname{sgn}(t)\leftrightarrow\pi\delta(\omega)+\frac1{j\omega}u(t)=21​+21​sgn(t)↔πδ(ω)+jω1​.

Periodic signals have impulse spectra

A periodic signal x(t)=∑kakejkω0tx(t)=\sum_ka_ke^{jk\omega_0t}x(t)=∑k​ak​ejkω0​t is not absolutely integrable, but each exponential transforms to an impulse, ejkω0t↔2πδ(ω−kω0)e^{jk\omega_0t}\leftrightarrow2\pi\delta(\omega-k\omega_0)ejkω0​t↔2πδ(ω−kω0​). So

X(jω)=2π∑k=−∞∞ak δ(ω−kω0).X(j\omega)=2\pi\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}a_k\,\delta(\omega-k\omega_0).X(jω)=2πk=−∞∑∞​ak​δ(ω−kω0​).

If one period is the pulse g(t)g(t)g(t), then ak=1TG(jkω0)a_k=\frac1TG(jk\omega_0)ak​=T1​G(jkω0​): the impulse strengths follow the single pulse's spectrum.

When does the transform exist? Dirichlet conditions

X(jω)X(j\omega)X(jω) exists, and the inverse converges to x(t)x(t)x(t) (to the midpoint at jumps), if:

  1. xxx is absolutely integrable: ∫−∞∞∣x(t)∣ dt<∞\int_{-\infty}^\infty|x(t)|\,dt<\infty∫−∞∞​∣x(t)∣dt<∞;
  2. xxx has finitely many maxima and minima in any finite interval;
  3. xxx has finitely many finite discontinuities in any finite interval.

These conditions are sufficient, not necessary. Constants, steps, sinusoids and periodic signals fail condition 1, yet have transforms if we allow impulses. Even sin⁡Wtπt\frac{\sin Wt}{\pi t}πtsinWt​ is not absolutely integrable but has the ordinary transform "rectangle".

Bandwidth

The bandwidth of a real signal is the width of the band of positive frequencies over which ∣X(jω)∣|X(j\omega)|∣X(jω)∣ is significant.

  • Strictly band-limited (X=0X=0X=0 for ∣ω∣>W|\omega|>W∣ω∣>W): the bandwidth is WWW.
  • Otherwise: an essential bandwidth, e.g. the first null, or the band holding 90–99% of the energy.

Narrower pulses, sharper edges and faster changes all mean larger bandwidth. δ(t)\delta(t)δ(t) has infinite bandwidth.

Applications: where the Fourier transform quietly appears

  • Audio denoising: voice sits at low and mid frequencies, hiss at high frequencies. Keep the useful band, reduce the rest.
  • Image denoising: noise hides in high spatial frequencies; a slightly blurry but clean image often beats a sharp noisy one.
  • JPEG compression: small high-frequency coefficients of each image block are rounded away; the eye barely notices.
  • MRI: the scanner measures frequency-domain data ("k-space") first; the image is reconstructed by an inverse transform.
  • Music recognition: a song is identified from the pattern of its strongest frequency peaks over time, a frequency fingerprint.
  • Vibration diagnosis: a cracked bearing or loose part changes a machine's spectrum before it is visible in time.
  • ECG filtering: remove 50 Hz power-line hum without destroying the heartbeat.

Exam pointers

  • Build unknown transforms from known pairs with properties, and name each property you use.
  • A spectrum given as magnitude and phase plots: write X=∣X∣ej∠XX=|X|e^{j\angle X}X=∣X∣ej∠X piece by piece. A phase of ±π/2\pm\pi/2±π/2 that flips sign at ω=0\omega=0ω=0 usually signals a factor jωj\omegajω (a derivative).
  • Shifted rectangles: transform the centred one, then multiply by e−jωt0e^{-j\omega t_0}e−jωt0​.
  • Watch the convention: ω\omegaω (with 12π\frac1{2\pi}2π1​ in the inverse) or fff (no 12π\frac1{2\pi}2π1​).
